name: Behavioural Experiment
lede: Anxiety makes predictions. This is a small, safe way to find out what actually happens — and to record the result before your memory rewrites it.
why: Reassurance rarely shifts a fear; evidence sometimes does. By naming the prediction, rating how likely it feels, doing one small ordinary thing, and then re-rating it, you collect your own data. Note that this worksheet never generates or ranks an experiment for you — you choose from safe, everyday options, and anything involving risk routes to real support instead.

steps.prompt: First — does this situation involve any of the following?
steps.help: Immediate danger · a medical symptom · someone hurting you · feeling unable to stay safe
steps.routeMessage: This isn't something to test in an exercise. That deserves real support, right now — not a worksheet.

steps.prompt: What are you afraid will happen?
steps.help: Be as specific as you can — vague fears are hard to test.
steps.placeholder: e.g. If I ask a question in the meeting, people will think I'm not up to the job

steps.prompt: How likely does that feel right now?
Pick a small, ordinary thing you could actually do
steps.help: Everyday and low-stakes on purpose. Choose the smallest one you'd genuinely try.
options: Ask one short question out loud
Send a message I've been putting off
Say no to one small request
Let one small mistake stand uncorrected

steps.help: A rough time is fine. You can always move it.

steps.title: Come back after
steps.body: The rest of this is for afterwards. Leave now and pick it up later — your answers are kept when you save at the end.

steps.help: What did you notice — in the room, and in you?
steps.placeholder: e.g. I asked. Someone said it was a good question. Nobody looked at me oddly.

steps.prompt: Knowing that — how likely does the feared thing feel now?
